questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a heavy nucleus gains on splitting
questions.learningObjective: state the energy reason a heavy nucleus releases energy when it splits
questions.stem: A heavy nucleus fissions into two medium nuclei of roughly half its mass. Why does that split release energy rather than absorb it?

options.text: The two fragments are more tightly bound per nucleon, so the difference appears as energy
The two fragments are less tightly bound per nucleon, so energy is needed to hold them
options.misconception: inverts the binding comparison, so a gain on the curve reads as a cost

options.text: The original nucleus had too few neutrons, so binding is released as they redistribute
options.misconception: credits the reaction to neutron excess rather than to binding per nucleon

options.text: The fragments move apart, and the kinetic energy of that motion comes from the barrier
options.misconception: credits the release to the Coulomb barrier rather than to the binding difference

questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon rises as a heavy nucleus is broken into mid-mass pieces, so the products sit lower on the binding curve and the difference in total binding energy is given back as kinetic energy and radiation. The reason is the same one that stops iron from fissioning: iron already sits at the peak, so there is no gain left to collect. Neutron excess and the Coulomb barrier both matter to whether the split happens, but neither is where the released energy comes from once it does.
questions.hint: Look at where a heavy nucleus and its mid-mass fragments sit on the binding curve.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the binding curve peaks near iron
questions.learningObjective: explain why fusion works below the peak and fission above it
questions.stem: Binding energy per nucleon climbs steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron, then falls slowly for heavy nuclei. Which pair of statements follows from that shape?

options.text: Fusing light nuclei releases energy, and splitting heavy nuclei also releases energy, but iron releases neither
Fusing light nuclei releases energy, while splitting heavy nuclei needs energy because the curve falls
options.misconception: reads a fall in the curve as an energy cost rather than a released gain

options.text: Iron can be fused for a profit and can be fissioned for a profit, since it sits at the maximum
options.misconception: believes a maximum on the curve means energy is available in both directions

options.text: Only fusion releases energy, and heavy nuclei release energy only when struck by a slow neutron
options.misconception: believes a triggering condition decides whether energy is released at all

questions.explanation: Energy is released whenever the products sit higher on the binding curve than the reactants, so light nuclei gain by fusing and heavy nuclei gain by splitting, and iron is the one size where neither route moves the system uphill on the curve. That is why a fusion reactor needs light fuel and why a fission reactor needs heavy fuel, and it is the whole reason the curve is drawn at all. Neither the trigger nor the mechanism of the reaction enters the accounting: a slow neutron is needed to make uranium split happen, not to make the split pay.
questions.hint: Ask which direction along the curve moves a system towards more binding.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: define the mass defect of a nucleus
questions.stem: The mass of a nucleus is measured to be smaller than the sum of the masses of the separate nucleons that make it up. What is that shortfall called?

options.text: The mass defect, which equals the binding energy divided by the speed of light squared
The mass defect, which is the energy needed to prise the nucleus back into free nucleons
options.misconception: calls an energy the mass defect, confusing the two roles in the relation

options.text: The mass defect, which shows the nucleus carries negative energy because it is lighter
options.misconception: believes a lighter nucleus must have negative rather than positive binding energy

options.text: The mass defect, which is the mass the nucleus loses as its charge spreads over the volume
options.misconception: blames the mass shortfall on the spread of charge rather than on binding

questions.explanation: The mass defect is the difference between the mass of the bound nucleus and the mass of its parts, and multiplying it by the speed of light squared gives the binding energy, so the two are the same fact in different units. It is positive, and it is the energy that must be supplied to pull the nucleus apart, which is why a tightly bound nucleus is hard to dismantle. It is not a negative energy, and it has nothing to do with the charge being spread out, since that affects the electric potential energy and not the mass.
questions.hint: One quantity in this description is an energy and the other is a mass difference.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What makes a chain reaction critical
questions.learningObjective: state the condition for a fission chain reaction to be self sustaining
questions.stem: Each uranium-235 fission in a reactor releases two or three neutrons. What must be true for the chain reaction to sustain itself at a steady rate?

options.text: On average each fission must cause about one further fission, and the rest are absorbed or lost
Every neutron released must cause a further fission, or the reaction will not be steady
options.misconception: requires every neutron to be productive, which no real design achieves

options.text: The number of neutrons released per fission must exceed two, whatever the losses
options.misconception: ignores losses entirely and mistakes surplus for criticality

options.text: The fuel must be kept below a temperature threshold so that fewer neutrons escape
options.misconception: makes criticality a matter of temperature rather than of neutron balance

questions.explanation: Criticality is a balance: the number of fissions per generation must stay the same, which means the average number of productive neutrons per fission has to be one once losses to absorption, leakage and non-fission captures are counted. Because some neutrons always go missing, a bare piece of uranium-235 with its natural two or three per fission would grow faster than one generation to the next, which is why a reactor needs a moderator, absorbers and control rods to sit exactly on the balance point. A temperature threshold is not part of the condition, and demanding that every neutron be productive would make the design impossible.
questions.hint: Count neutrons in and neutrons lost, generation by generation.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state the job of a moderator in a thermal reactor
questions.stem: A thermal reactor places ordinary water or graphite around the fuel. What is that surrounding material for?

options.text: To slow neutrons down, because slow neutrons are far more likely to be captured by a fuel nucleus
To slow neutrons down so that they lose energy to the escaping radiation of the core
options.misconception: misdescribes where the neutron energy actually goes in a moderator

options.text: To absorb excess neutrons and hold the reaction steady without any control rods at all
options.misconception: describes an absorber, which is the opposite of what a moderator does

options.text: To cool the fuel so that it can run at a lower temperature without losing neutrons
options.misconception: confuses the cooling duty with the neutron-slowing duty

questions.explanation: Uranium-235 absorbs a slow neutron far more readily than a fast one, and fission fragments leave the split with energies of the order of a megavolt, so a fresh generation starts too energetic to sustain the chain. Passing through a light nucleus repeatedly in elastic collisions bleeds that energy off cheaply, which is why water and graphite work and heavy materials do not. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods and of the borated water in some designs, and cooling the fuel is a separate duty that happens in the same circuit but serves a different purpose.
questions.hint: Compare the probability that a fuel nucleus absorbs a slow neutron with a fast one.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: identify what determines the radiation dose a patient receives
questions.stem: A patient's dose depends on several quantities. Which grouping correctly separates the ones that change it?

options.text: Energy absorbed per unit mass, the type of radiation, and how long and how close the exposure lasts
The total energy of the source alone, since more energy in the machine means a larger dose
options.misconception: confuses the energy a source holds with the energy a patient absorbs

options.text: The activity of the source and the distance only, since those two set every dose figure
options.misconception: believes source strength and distance are the only things a dose depends on

options.text: The mass of the patient alone, since dose is energy divided by the mass of the equipment
options.misconception: uses the equipment mass in a definition that calls for the patient mass

questions.explanation: Dose is energy absorbed per unit mass of tissue, so it depends on how much energy the tissue actually takes, and how much it takes is set by the radiation type, since alpha and neutron radiation deposit far more energy per unit path than X-rays or gamma rays do. Exposure time and distance matter too, because a field falls off with the inverse square of the distance, so doubling the distance quarters the dose rate. A source's total energy says nothing about how much is deposited in one patient, and the mass in the definition is the patient's, not the equipment's.
questions.hint: Start from the definition of dose and ask what each factor in it controls.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the physical half-life from the biological half-life
questions.stem: An isotope used in treatment has a physical half-life of eight days, while the body clears it with a biological half-life of four days. Which statement describes the combined behaviour?

options.text: Both removal routes act at once, so the combined half-life is shorter than either one alone
The faster route takes over completely, so the combined half-life equals the shorter one exactly
options.misconception: believes the slower removal route stops acting once the faster one begins

options.text: The two routes act in sequence, so the combined half-life adds to fourteen days
options.misconception: treats two simultaneous processes as steps taken one after another

options.text: The two routes are unrelated, so the combined half-life is the average of the two values
options.misconception: averages two half-lives, which has no physical basis at all

questions.explanation: Radioactive decay and biological clearance both remove the isotope from wherever it is being measured, and they do it simultaneously and independently, so their rates add and the combined half-life is shorter than either. With eight and four days the result is 2.4 days, not four, because clearing by the body is already well under way while the nuclei are still decaying. Treating the routes as alternatives in sequence would put the total at twelve days, which is far too long, and averaging the two has no physical basis at all.
questions.hint: Both processes act on the same population at the same time, so add their rates.

questions.topic: What each imaging method resolves best
questions.learningObjective: match an imaging method to the contrast it resolves best
questions.stem: An X-ray image, an ultrasound scan and a nuclear medicine scan are available for the same patient. Which contrast does each resolve best?

options.text: X-rays for dense bone, ultrasound for soft tissue, and a tracer for where a specific molecule goes
X-rays for soft tissue, ultrasound for bone, and a tracer for motion at any depth
options.misconception: assigns each contrast to the wrong method

options.text: X-rays for the chemical state of a tissue, ultrasound for the stop of light
options.misconception: assigns chemical contrast to X-rays and gives light behaviour to sound

options.text: X-rays for motion, ultrasound for chemical state, and a tracer for bone density alone
options.misconception: misassigns all three contrasts to the wrong methods

questions.explanation: The contrast comes from what the method interacts with: X-rays are absorbed in proportion to density and atomic number, so bone stands out against soft tissue, while ultrasound is reflected by boundaries between tissues and so images the internal structure of soft organs. A tracer image comes from a labelled molecule, and the image then records where that molecule went rather than the density of anything. None of the three reports the chemical state of a tissue directly, so an answer built on that cannot be right on any of the three counts.
questions.hint: Ask what each method interacts with inside the body.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a track rather than a point
questions.learningObjective: explain why a particle detector records a track rather than a single point
questions.stem: A detector used in a particle experiment registers a continuous line of ionisation rather than a single dot, and a photograph taken from the side shows the line. Why is a track the useful record?

options.text: The path fixes the direction of travel, and the density of ionisation along it fixes the energy loss rate
The path fixes the speed of the particle, and the length of the line fixes its lifetime in seconds
options.misconception: reads a track as a timing record rather than a path and an energy record

options.text: The path shows only that something passed, and the density of the line is set by the detector gain
options.misconception: dismisses the density as a gain artefact rather than as energy loss

options.text: The path shows the identity of the particle, since a curved track is unique to one species
options.misconception: believes the shape alone identifies the particle without any measurement

questions.explanation: A track is a record of a path in space, so its curvature in a known field gives the momentum, and the spacing of the ionisation along it gives the rate of energy loss, which is a fingerprint of the particle type and a way to estimate its energy. Both pieces of information are lost if only a count of hits is kept. The length of a line is a distance and needs a speed to become a time, and the shape of a track is suggestive rather than identifying, since a short track and a weak one can look much alike.
questions.hint: Ask what curvature measures and what the spacing between deposits measures.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why radiation detectors are sited deep underground
questions.stem: A neutrino or rare-decay experiment is sited a kilometre of rock below the surface rather than on the ground. What does the overburden accomplish?

options.text: It absorbs nearly all the incoming cosmic radiation before it can reach the detector
It keeps the detector at a steady temperature so the electronics give fewer false signals
options.misconception: credits the overburden with temperature control rather than shielding

options.text: It blocks the neutrinos themselves, so only the ones produced underground are counted
options.misconception: believes rock stops neutrinos, which would defeat the purpose of the experiment

options.text: It reflects any radiation that gets past, sending it back for a second interaction
options.misconception: expects shielding to reflect radiation back into the chamber

questions.explanation: Cosmic ray muons are the most penetrating component of the background, and a kilometre of rock attenuates them by many orders of magnitude, which is the only way to see a signal that occurs once a year. The rock is chosen for that attenuation, not for temperature, although a stable underground site does help with electronics. Neutrinos pass through rock almost unhindered, which is the whole point of the siting, and nothing underground reflects the surviving radiation back into the chamber.
questions.hint: Compare how well rock attenuates cosmic muons and neutrinos.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The two laws constraining a spectrum
questions.learningObjective: name the two laws that fix the total and peak of a blackbody spectrum
questions.stem: A hot cavity is measured to emit a continuous spectrum. Which pair of results is enough to predict both how much power leaves the cavity and where the spectrum peaks?

options.text: The total radiated power per unit area from the fourth power of the temperature, and the peak wavelength from the inverse of the temperature
The total power from the square of the temperature, and the peak wavelength from the temperature itself
options.misconception: uses a square law for the power and a direct law for the peak

options.text: The total power from the inverse of the temperature, and the peak wavelength from the square of it
options.misconception: inverts the power law and squares the peak law, changing both dependencies

options.text: The total power from the fourth power of the temperature, and the peak wavelength from that same power
options.misconception: tries to read the peak wavelength out of the total power instead of the temperature

questions.explanation: One law ties the power radiated per unit area to the fourth power of the absolute temperature, with a constant of proportionality, and the other ties the wavelength of the peak of the spectral curve to the inverse of the temperature, again with a constant. Between them they fix the size of the curve and where on the wavelength axis it sits, which is why a hotter cavity both radiates far more power and shifts towards shorter wavelengths. A square law or an inverse law would break the observed sensitivity to temperature, and the peak wavelength is a property of the temperature rather than of the total power.
questions.hint: One of the two laws is a power law and the other is an inverse law.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what a background radiation temperature implies about the early universe
questions.stem: A background of microwave radiation is detected in every direction, uniform to a few parts in a hundred thousand, at a temperature of 2.7 K. What does that measurement establish about the universe?

options.text: The universe began in a hot, dense state, and the radiation has cooled by stretching as space expanded
The universe is still radiating at 2.7 K from its centre, and the waves have simply arrived intact
options.misconception: believes the universe has been radiating at the present temperature all along

options.text: The universe cooled to 2.7 K and stayed there, with no expansion and no radiation since
options.misconception: keeps a hot origin but denies the expansion that would cool the radiation

options.text: Stars are collectively so faint that they have cooled the whole sky to 2.7 K
options.misconception: credits starlight rather than a relic with the measured brightness

questions.explanation: A hot early state followed by expansion cools radiation exactly as it cools a gas, by stretching the wavelengths, and a blackbody spectrum with a 2.7 K temperature is the fossil of that cooling rather than of any present source. The near uniformity is itself the evidence, because that is what inflation predicts for a universe that was once much smaller, so a hotter fireball that has not expanded is ruled out. Stars cannot account for it, since the measured brightness is that of a 2.7 K blackbody and the source would be the stars themselves, which are nowhere near filling the sky at that level.
questions.hint: Ask what expansion does to the wavelength of radiation already present.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: interpret a redshift as evidence that distant objects recede
questions.stem: Spectra from distant galaxies show every line shifted to a longer wavelength than the same line measured in the laboratory. What does that shift indicate?

options.text: The space between us and the galaxy has stretched, carrying the light along as it travelled
The light lost energy to intergalactic dust, so the photons arrived with a longer wavelength
options.misconception: believes a selective loss in dust can shift every line by the same factor

options.text: The galaxy is cooling, so its atomic lines are emitted at longer wavelengths than in the laboratory
options.misconception: blames the emitter rather than the intervening space for the shift

options.text: The light is crossing a gravitational field, so it has fallen to a lower frequency
options.misconception: uses gravitational redshift, which is far too small on this scale

questions.explanation: All the lines of a distant source shift by the same factor, not by the same absolute amount, which is the signature of a stretching of the space the light travelled through rather than of any selective loss. Dust and cooling would act on particular wavelengths or particular atoms, so the pattern would be distorted rather than uniformly scaled. A gravitational effect exists but is tiny on intergalactic scales, so the systematic increase of shift with distance is what identifies the expansion itself.
questions.hint: Check whether every line is shifted by the same fraction or by the same amount.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The content of the expansion law
questions.learningObjective: state the content and units of the expansion law
questions.stem: Recession speed grows in proportion to distance, with a constant near 70 kilometres per second for each megaparsec. What does the constant represent, and what are its units?

options.text: The present rate of expansion per unit distance, in reciprocal seconds
The present age of the universe, quoted in seconds per unit distance
options.misconception: confuses the reciprocal age with the rate per unit distance

options.text: The speed of the nearest galaxies divided by their distance, in kilometres per second
options.misconception: expects the constant to be a speed rather than a rate per distance

options.text: The rate at which the expansion constant itself grows, in reciprocal seconds per year
options.misconception: answers with the change in the constant rather than the constant itself

questions.explanation: Dividing the speed by the distance leaves a quantity with units of reciprocal time, and its value today is about 70 kilometres per second for each megaparsec, which is the quantity used to turn a redshift into a distance. Taking the reciprocal of that constant gives the approximate age of the universe, because a constant expansion rate can be traced back to zero size, so age and rate are related but are not the same number. The constant is not itself a speed, and its rate of change is a separate and much more delicate measurement.
questions.hint: Divide a speed by the distance it goes with and look at what units survive.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state which observed abundances nucleosynthesis explains
questions.stem: The abundances of helium and the heavier elements in the oldest stars can be measured. Which statement about explaining those abundances is correct?

options.text: Nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes accounts for the helium and traces of deuterium
Nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes accounts for all the helium and all the heavier elements
options.misconception: claims the early universe made every element, leaving nothing for stars to do

options.text: Nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes accounts for the heavier elements but not the helium
options.misconception: assigns the two families the wrong way round

options.text: Nucleosynthesis in the first few minutes accounts for nothing, since all of it came later in stars
options.misconception: denies the early reaction chain that the primordial helium requires

questions.explanation: The first few minutes were hot and dense enough for protons and neutrons to fuse, and the reaction chain stopped as soon as the universe cooled below the temperature at which deuterium could survive, so it left a specific and calculable fraction of helium with traces of deuterium and lithium behind. Claiming all the heavier elements would erase the need for stars altogether, which the abundance of elements beyond lithium in old stars contradicts.

questions.topic: The balance in a stable star
questions.learningObjective: state the competing terms that balance in a stable star
questions.stem: A main sequence star holds a steady spherical shape for millions of years. Which pair of effects is in balance?

options.text: Gravity pulling every layer inward, against the pressure gradient pushing outward from the hot interior
The pull of gravity inward, against the outward flow of the fusion products in the wind
options.misconception: credits a weak stellar wind with supporting the whole star

options.text: The outward radiation pressure, against the inward pull of the magnetic field in the core
options.misconception: puts a magnetic field where the competing term should be gas pressure

options.text: The inward pull of gravity, against the outward centrifugal force from the rotation
options.misconception: offers rotation as the term that balances gravity in most stars

questions.explanation: Every layer of the star is pulled in by the gravity of everything outside it and pushed out by the pressure gradient of the hot gas, and the star holds its size while those two balance at every radius. The pressure exists because the core is hot enough to keep fusing, and if the fusion stopped the pressure would fall and the core would contract. A stellar wind is far too weak to shape the star, and there is no dynamically important magnetic field in the core to balance anything, while rotation does matter for some stars but is not what sets the overall pressure balance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the energy released by a fission from a mass balance
questions.stem: One uranium-235 nucleus of mass 235.0439 u absorbs a neutron of mass 1.0087 u and splits into barium-144 of mass 143.9227 u, krypton-89 of mass 88.9176 u and three neutrons of mass 1.0087 u each. Using 1 u of mass corresponding to 931.5 MeV of energy, what energy is released, in MeV? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The incoming mass is 235.0439 plus 1.0087, which is 236.0526 u, and the outgoing mass is 143.9227 plus 88.9176 plus 3.0261, which is 235.8664 u, so the mass defect is 0.1862 u. Multiplying by 931.5 MeV per u gives 173.4 MeV, and the terms are best subtracted in groups as well, which arrives at the same figure. The typical figure quoted for a fission event is of this order, and adding rather than subtracting the masses would report a mass gain where a defect is required.
questions.hint: Total the masses on each side of the reaction before subtracting.

questions.learningObjective: estimate the collisions needed to slow a neutron to thermal speeds
questions.stem: A fission neutron of 2.0e6 eV is slowed by elastic collisions with carbon nuclei of mass number 12 until it reaches 2.5e-2 eV. Taking the average energy retained after each collision as the quantity 0.716, about how many collisions are needed? Use 2.302 for the natural logarithm of 10. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The ratio of the starting energy to the final energy is 8.0e7, whose natural logarithm is 2.302 times 7 plus 2.302 times 0.85, or 16.1 plus 1.96, giving about 18.1. Each collision multiplies the energy by 0.716, so the logarithm of the reciprocal of 0.716, which is 0.334, is the logarithm lost per collision, and 18.1 over 0.334 gives 54.5 collisions. Taking the reciprocal of 0.716 instead of its logarithm would compare logarithms wrongly, and this is why light nuclei are the useful moderator materials: they shed a large fraction of the energy each time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: How a spectrum moves with temperature
questions.learningObjective: predict how a peak wavelength changes as a source heats up
questions.stem: A cavity is measured at three temperatures, with its spectrum peaking at 10.0, 5.0 and 2.0 micrometres. What do those peaks imply about the temperatures used?

options.text: Each doubling of temperature moved the peak to half the wavelength, at 290, 580 and 1160 K
Each halving of temperature moved the peak to half the wavelength, at 1160, 580 and 290 K
options.misconception: has the direction of the temperature dependence the wrong way round

options.text: The temperatures are 290, 58 and 12 K, falling as the peak moved to shorter waves
options.misconception: loses a factor of ten on the shorter wavelengths, as though the units were mixed

options.text: The temperature is fixed at 290 K and only the detector gain changed between runs
options.misconception: credits gain with a change that moves a real wavelength

questions.explanation: The displacement law makes the peak wavelength inversely proportional to the temperature, so a peak moving from 10.0 to 5.0 micrometres is a doubling of the temperature, and dividing 2.898e-3 metre kelvin by each wavelength gives 290, 580 and 1160 kelvin. That is the behaviour of any hot body, and it is the reason a star's colour is a temperature readout and the reason a background spectrum can be turned into a single number. Reading the same pattern as falling temperature would have the direction of the dependence backwards, and a change of gain would move no wavelength at all.
questions.hint: Divide the displacement constant by each peak wavelength to get the temperature.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: A rotation curve that stays flat
questions.learningObjective: interpret a flat orbital speed curve as evidence for unseen mass
questions.stem: The orbital speed of a galaxy is measured at 5, 10, 20 and 40 thousand light years from its centre, giving 150, 175, 195 and 200 kilometres per second. What does that pattern indicate?

options.text: Mass spread well beyond the visible stars, since enclosed mass should otherwise fall with radius
A central mass only, since a point mass at the centre produces a flat speed curve
options.misconception: believes a point mass gives a flat curve, where it actually gives a falling one

options.text: No extended mass at all, since the speeds are too similar to be gravitational
options.misconception: reads a flat curve as evidence against gravity rather than for more mass

options.text: A distribution of stars so sparse that the galaxy is mostly empty at large radius
options.misconception: concludes emptiness rather than unseen mass from the same readings

questions.explanation: For a spherical system the speed of a circular orbit rises as the square root of the mass enclosed so far, so if the bright central region held everything the outermost orbits would have to be much slower than the inner ones, and this fall in enclosed mass is not what the readings show. The flat curve means the enclosed mass is still growing with radius well outside the visible light, which is the standard evidence for a dark component rather than for an absence of mass. A point mass at the centre would give a speed that falls with distance rather than staying level, and the curve remains a gravitational one either way.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to the speed if the enclosed mass stopped growing with radius.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: A claimed signal inside the uncertainty
questions.learningObjective: judge a claimed deviation that is smaller than the measurement uncertainty
questions.stem: An expansion constant is measured as 70.0 plus or minus 3.0 kilometres per second for each megaparsec, and the reciprocal of a neighbouring measurement gives an age of 13.0 plus or minus 0.7 billion years. What can be said about a claim that the universe is 0.4 billion years younger than that?

options.text: The claim lies inside the uncertainty, so the data do not distinguish it from the central value
The claim is confirmed, since any shift of that size is a real change in the constant
options.misconception: calls an effect smaller than the error bar a confirmed change

options.text: The claim is refuted, since a genuine age cannot differ from the measurement at all
options.misconception: demands that a real quantity match a noisy measurement exactly

options.text: The claim is confirmed, because 0.4 billion years exceeds the quoted 0.07 billion year resolution
options.misconception: treats decimal places as though they were precision

questions.explanation: The claimed shift of 0.4 billion years is smaller than the plus or minus 0.7 billion year uncertainty on the age, so the measurement is perfectly consistent with it and cannot pick it out from noise. A genuine deviation has to stand clear of the error bar before it means anything, and quoting the central value to two significant figures hides the spread entirely. The resolution in the last option is a decimal-place artefact rather than a precision of the measurement, and no deviation becomes real by being small or by being quoted neatly.
questions.hint: Compare the size of the claimed effect with the size of the uncertainty.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why a reactor needs a moderator
questions.learningObjective: explain why neutrons must be slowed before they can sustain a chain reaction
questions.stem: Fission fragments leave a split with energies of the order of a megavolt, yet the fuel absorbs slow neutrons far more readily than fast ones. Explain why a reactor cannot simply use the neutrons as they come out, and what the moderator does about it.

answer.exemplar: The chance that a uranium nucleus will absorb a neutron is strongly dependent on how slowly the neutron is travelling, and a neutron fresh from a split is far too energetic to be captured easily. If the fuel had to make do with those fast neutrons, each generation of fissions would produce far fewer fissions than the generation before, and the chain would die out however much fuel was present. A moderator fixes this by repeatedly colliding the neutrons with light nuclei, and because an elastic collision with a light nucleus can transfer a large fraction of the neutron's energy, a few dozen collisions bring the energies down into the thermal range where capture is likely. The moderator is neither a source of neutrons nor a coolant, and the design problem is to slow the neutrons without absorbing too many of them, which is why the choice of material cannot be pushed further than its nuclear properties allow.

questions.explanation: The capture probability falls steeply with neutron energy, so a chain that starts with fast neutrons dies out. The moderator buys the energy loss in elastic collisions, and it has to do that without eating the neutrons.
questions.hint: Compare the capture probability for a fast and a slow neutron in the same fuel.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the biological half-life of a tracer differs from its physical half-life
questions.stem: A tracer used in a medical scan has a physical half-life set by its nucleus and a biological half-life set by the body. Explain why the two are different quantities, and what happens to the tracer's presence when both act at once.

answer.exemplar: The physical half-life is a property of the nucleus alone, fixed by the decay probability per unit time, and it would be the same whatever happened to the patient. The biological half-life is a property of the body, fixed by how quickly the tracer is carried away, broken down or excreted, and it can differ enormously between patients for the same isotope. Because the two act on the same population at the same time and independently, their rates add, so the effective half-life is the reciprocal of the sum of the two rates and is always shorter than either one alone. That is what makes the dose from a tracer predictable: the activity decays as the nuclei decay, while the amount of tracer in the body falls faster still, and a patient with a poor circulation is therefore irradiated for less time than the physics of the nucleus alone would suggest.

questions.explanation: One quantity belongs to the nucleus and the other to the patient, and because they act simultaneously the combined half-life is shorter than either. The rate bookkeeping, not a choice between the two, gives the effective value.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two quantities would change if the patient changed but the isotope did not.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Inferring a black hole without seeing it
questions.learningObjective: explain how a black hole is identified from effects rather than from direct sight
questions.stem: A black hole emits no light, so an astronomer argues for one on the basis of what can be measured around it. Explain the chain of reasoning, and say which parts of it are direct measurements rather than assumptions.

answer.exemplar: The starting point is direct: gas orbiting the centre of the galaxy is observed, and the speeds of those orbits can be turned into the amount of mass that must be enclosed at each radius. Inside the orbit of the innermost star there is no visible object at all, and the measured speeds near the centre are far too large for the mass of the stars and gas that are actually there, so the enclosed mass has to rise steeply in a region with no light. That much is inference from measurement. Moving from a large unseen mass to a black hole adds two further steps: the object must be compact enough, from the radii of the orbits, that light cannot escape it, and it must be packed into a small volume, since the same mass spread widely would be luminous. Where those conditions hold, a star moving at those speeds is the observable signature, and no image of the object itself is required or possible.

questions.explanation: Orbital speeds and orbit radii give the mass, the mass and the extent give the compactness, and the compactness gives the escape failure. The light curves are measurements; the object at the centre is an inference drawn from them.
questions.hint: Separate the measured orbital quantities from the conclusions drawn about what they imply.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how overburden reduces the count rate in an underground detector
questions.stem: A rare-event experiment is moved a kilometre underground and the background count rate falls by a factor of a thousand or more. Explain how that reduction is achieved, and why the same rock does not block the particles the experiment is looking for.

answer.exemplar: The dominant background at the surface is not the radioactivity of the rock but the secondary particles made when high-energy cosmic rays hit the atmosphere. Those products are mostly muons, and a muon is a very penetrating particle, so it will pass through a kilometre of rock only with a small probability, whereas a detector at the surface intercepts essentially all of them. Because the attenuation grows exponentially with depth, a modest increase in overburden multiplies the reduction, which is how a modest experiment reaches a usable signal to background ratio. Neutrinos, the particles such an experiment wants, interact so weakly that a kilometre of rock stops essentially none of them, so the signal survives while the background does not, and the price is that only the surviving flux can be studied. The rock's own radioactivity is a second, smaller background, removed by making the surrounding material inert.

questions.explanation: The surface background is atmospheric secondaries, and depth attenuates them exponentially, while neutrinos pass through. Depth is a filter, not a wall.
questions.hint: Identify what the muons at the surface were made by, and how strongly rock attenuates them.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What holds a white dwarf up
questions.learningObjective: explain the support of a white dwarf and what the mass limit means for it
questions.stem: A white dwarf is a star with no fuel left, yet it does not collapse. Explain what holds it up, why that support fails past a certain mass, and what the failure produces instead.

answer.exemplar: The support comes from the electrons. A star of that size has far too little room for its electrons, and since electrons are fermions they cannot all occupy the same low states, so they are forced into higher and higher momentum states as the density rises, and the pressure of that crowded motion is enormous. That is the same uncertainty relation that limits a localising measurement, applied to a whole star, and it needs no heat source, which is why a white dwarf is stable with no fusion running. The support is not unlimited, though, because the electron pressure grows only as the four-thirds power of the density while gravity grows faster than the cube of the radius, so at some mass the inward pull wins for good. That mass is near one and a half times the Sun for a typical composition, and a star above it cannot settle into any static state, so it collapses until the neutrons take over and a neutron star forms, or continues to the point where escape fails and a black hole forms.

questions.explanation: Electron degeneracy pressure scales more slowly than gravity, so there is a mass at which it can no longer hold the star up, and a different kind of matter or a collapse is the outcome past that point.
questions.hint: Compare how the electron pressure grows with density against how gravity grows with size.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how a low background temperature is evidence for an early hot universe
questions.stem: Microwave radiation at 2.7 K fills the sky uniformly to a few parts in a hundred thousand. Explain how that measurement supports a universe that began hot, and say why uniformity and temperature are the two features to focus on.

answer.exemplar: The spectrum is close to that of an ideal radiator at 2.7 kelvin, which fixes the physical interpretation: this is thermal radiation, and thermal radiation at that temperature is what remains from a much hotter state once it has been cooled. Expansion cools radiation the same way it cools a gas, by stretching every wavelength, and no other process available today would produce a spectrum of exactly this shape filling every direction. The temperature is the part that records the cooling, and the near uniformity is the part that constrains the history, because points that are now widely separated were once close together, and a universe that began in a hot dense state would have had time for heat to spread between them. A hot beginning not followed by a large expansion would leave a background far hotter than this, and a universe that expanded too late to mix would show variation between opposite directions, which is not observed.

questions.explanation: The spectrum identifies the radiation as thermal, the temperature records how far it has cooled, and the uniformity is the constraint on how well the early universe mixed.
questions.hint: Ask what expansion does to radiation already present, and what the uniformity rules out.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: From fission to a controlled reaction
questions.learningObjective: order the chain from a fission event to a controlled self sustaining reaction
questions.stem: Four statements trace the reasoning from a single fission to a reactor running at a steady power. Put them in the order in which they follow, earliest first.

options.text: Absorbers and control rods are set so that the average of the two or three neutrons becomes one
A heavy nucleus absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two mid-mass fragments plus neutrons
Those fragments are more tightly bound per nucleon, and the difference leaves as energy
The extra neutrons are slowed until they are likely to be absorbed, closing the chain

questions.explanation: The physical event comes first, since nothing can be controlled until there is a reaction to control, and the energy source is the second step because the release follows from where the products sit on the binding curve. Criticality is a counting step over generations, and that is where the absorbers enter, because the average number of neutrons causing a further fission has to be one rather than two or three. Only then does the slowing step complete the picture, since without neutrons in the energy range where capture is likely there would be nothing to keep in the chain at all.
questions.hint: Energy release before criticality, and slowing only once the chain is to be sustained.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Working a binding energy from a table
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that turn tabulated masses into a binding energy per nucleon
questions.stem: Four statements describe how a binding energy per nucleon is obtained from tabulated masses. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: That mass defect is multiplied by 931.5 MeV per unit mass to give the total binding energy
The mass of the nucleus is read from the table, together with its proton and neutron counts
The result is divided by the total number of nucleons, which is the proton count plus the neutron count
Hydrogen atom and neutron masses are combined to give the mass of the separate parts

questions.explanation: The counts and the measured mass have to be in hand before any arithmetic can start, and the mass of the separate parts is built from the tabulated hydrogen atom and neutron masses, where using hydrogen rather than bare protons is what cancels the electron masses. The shortfall between the two is the mass defect, and only then can the conversion turn it into an energy. The division by the nucleon count is the last step and not the first, and doing it first produces a number larger than the total binding energy, which is a clear sign that the per-nucleon label has been mishandled.
questions.hint: Counts and mass first, then the separate parts, then the defect, then the division.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: From a redshift to a distance
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that turn a measured redshift into a distance estimate
questions.stem: Four statements describe how a measured redshift becomes a distance estimate. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The recession speed is divided by the expansion constant to give the distance in megaparsecs
The wavelength of a known spectral line in the source is compared with its laboratory value
The result is compared with the age implied by the reciprocal of the same constant
The ratio of the two wavelengths is turned into a recession speed, valid here because it is small

questions.explanation: A redshift is a ratio of two wavelengths, so the measurement has to be made before anything can be calculated from it, and for a small redshift that ratio converts into a speed by multiplying by the speed of light. The speed is not a distance, so the expansion constant is needed to scale it, and once the distance is in hand the same constant can be inverted to give an approximate age for comparison. The order of the last two can be exchanged without changing the physics, but both must follow the speed, since neither the age nor the distance can be reached from a wavelength ratio alone.
questions.hint: Measure the ratio, convert it to a speed, then use the constant for the distance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What a black hole claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: order the inferential steps that turn a measured orbital speed into a black hole claim
questions.stem: Four statements trace the inference from a measured orbital speed to a claim about a black hole. Put them in the order in which the reasoning runs, earliest first.

options.text: The orbit radii show the mass lies inside a very small volume, so light cannot escape it
The speed at each orbital radius is measured directly from the spectrum of the orbiting gas
The unexplained mass is not luminous, so the alternatives of dim stars or gas are excluded
That enclosed mass is compared with the mass of the visible stars and gas at the same radius

questions.explanation: The only direct measurements here are the speeds and the orbit radii, so they come first, and the first thing done with them is to convert a speed at a radius into the mass that must be enclosed inside that radius. Only then can the enclosed mass be compared with what is actually visible, and a large shortfall has to be accounted for before anything more exotic is proposed. Excluding the ordinary explanations for that shortfall comes before the final step, because a compact but luminous object would not be a black hole even with the same mass. The compactness argument is last because it depends on all the earlier conclusions.
questions.hint: Measurements, then the mass they imply, then what is missing, then what that rules in.
